summary: Some networks, such as those carrying financial market data, care about performance measures like latency as much as other path constraints. This document extends PCEP so such service-related metrics can be requested, and used when computing label switched paths.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8233 lets a path planner be told what matters besides cost. A client can ask for a path whose delay, delay variation, packet loss or link bandwidth use stays under a limit, or ask for the path that minimises one of those. The Path Computation Element then computes the path with the new constraints and reports the values it found.

subtitle: PCEP learns to ask for paths by latency, delay variation, packet loss and link utilization, not just by cost.

tldr.problem: Some networks, such as financial data networks, must pick paths by performance measures like latency tied to a service level agreement, but PCEP had no standard way to ask for them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds six METRIC types for path delay, delay variation and loss, for both point-to-point and point-to-multipoint trees, a new BU object that caps link bandwidth utilization, and three new objective functions, plus the error handling for PCEs that cannot do it.
tldr.outcome: A client can bound or optimize a path by these measures, and a PCE can report the values it computed or the constraint it could not meet. RFC 9756 later updated this document.

today: RFC 8233 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 9756. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Paths Need Performance Constraints
sections.content:
Real-time network performance information is becoming critical to path computation in some networks. Mechanisms to measure latency, delay variation and packet loss in an MPLS network are described in RFC 6374. It matters that these values are taken into account during path selection, even before the label switched path is set up.

Link bandwidth utilization based on real-time traffic along the path is also becoming critical during path computation, so the utilization has to be factored in as well.

The Traffic Engineering Database (TED) is populated with network performance information such as link latency, delay variation and packet loss, along with bandwidth parameters, through the TE Metric Extensions in OSPF or IS-IS or through a management system. RFC 7823 describes how a Path Computation Element can use that information when selecting paths for explicitly routed LSPs.

A Path Computation Client (PCC) can ask a PCE for a path that meets end-to-end network performance criteria. This document extends the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) of RFC 5440 to handle constraints on any combination of latency, delay variation, packet loss and bandwidth utilization.
sections.plainLanguage: Some networks care about how fast and how reliable a path is, not only about its cost. The routers already collect that data in a traffic engineering database. This RFC lets a client ask the path computation element for a path with limits on delay, delay variation, packet loss or bandwidth use.

sections.title: Terms and Acronyms
sections.content:
The RFC uses these terms. IGP is an interior gateway protocol, either OSPF or IS-IS. LBU is Link Bandwidth Utilization and LRBU is Link Reserved Bandwidth Utilization. MPLP is the Minimum Packet Loss Path, MUP the Maximum Under-Utilized Path and MRUP the Maximum Reserved Under-Utilized Path, the last three being objective functions.

An objective function (OF) is a set of one or more optimization criteria used to compute a single path, such as path cost minimization, or a synchronized set of paths. A PCC is a path computation client, any application that asks a path computation element for a path. A PCE is a path computation element, an entity such as a component, an application or a network node that can compute a network path from a network graph while applying computational constraints. RSVP is the Resource Reservation Protocol, TE is traffic engineering, and the TED is the traffic engineering database.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC names the pieces of the system. The PCC is the client that asks for a path, the PCE is the element that computes it, and the TED is the database of link information the PCE reads. An objective function is the rule the PCE follows when it picks between several possible paths.

sections.title: New Metric Types
sections.content:
The METRIC object of RFC 5440 holds a metric value and a metric type in the T field, plus a flags field with the B bit and the P bit. This document defines six new types: T=12 for the Path Delay metric, T=13 for Path Delay Variation, T=14 for Path Loss, and T=15, T=16 and T=17 for the same three measures on a point-to-multipoint tree.

The Path Delay metric is the sum of the link delay of every link along a point-to-point path. The Path Delay Variation metric is the sum of the average delay variation of every link along the path. The Path Loss metric is a function of the unidirectional loss of every link: the percentage path loss is 1 minus the product of the survival probability of each link, times 100. For a point-to-multipoint tree, each of the three measures is the worst value among all the destinations in the tree.

A PCC may use these metrics in a Path Computation Request. With the B bit set, the metric value is a bound, a maximum that the computed path must not exceed for the PCC to accept it. With the B bit cleared, the metric asks the PCE to optimize that measure. A PCE may send the metric back in a Path Computation Reply, both with an Explicit Route Object to report the value it computed, and with a NO-PATH object when it cannot find a path that meets the constraint.

The metric value is a 32-bit IEEE floating point number. The link attributes that feed it are advertised in 24-bit integer fields, in microseconds for delay and delay variation and in percent for loss, so the conversion can lose some precision.
sections.plainLanguage: Six new metric types let a request carry a limit or a goal for delay, delay variation or packet loss, for a single path or for a tree of paths. Delay and delay variation add up along the path. Loss combines the links, because a packet has to survive every one of them. For a tree, the value is the worst of the paths to the destinations.

sections.title: How the Metrics Are Used and Refused
sections.content:
In a Path Computation Request a PCC may insert one or more METRIC objects, either to name the metric the computation must optimize or to give a bound that must not be exceeded. In a reply the PCE may insert a METRIC object with an Explicit Route Object to report the metric of the computed path, and with a NO-PATH object to say which constraint could not be satisfied. How the PCE optimizes for a metric is outside the scope of the RFC.

The RFC works through an example. If the metric to optimize is path delay and path loss must not exceed M, the request carries two METRIC objects: the first with B=0, T=12, C=1 and metric value 0x0000, and the second with B=1, T=14 and metric value M. If the PCE finds a path and no policy stops it, the reply carries one METRIC object with B=0, T=12 and the computed path delay, and may carry a second with B=1, T=14 and the computed path loss.

When a PCE does not understand a new metric type and the P bit is clear, it ignores the METRIC object. When the P bit is set and the type is not understood, the PCE must send an error message with Error-Type 4 and Error-value 4. When the type is understood but not supported, it must send Error-Type 4 with Error-value 5 and cancel the request. When local policy forbids the constraint, it must send Error-Type 5 with Error-value 8 and cancel the request.

The same rules apply across domains. The new metric types can be used for end-to-end path computation in the same way as the existing IGP or TE metrics, and the BU object can be used like a METRIC object with its B bit set. All domains must have the same understanding of the metrics, otherwise some form of metric normalization as described in RFC 5441 must be applied.
sections.plainLanguage: A request can carry several metric objects, one for the value to improve and another for the limit to respect. The reply reports what the PCE computed, or reports a NO-PATH object when it could not meet the limit. If the PCE does not understand the new metric, it ignores it, or returns an error when the client asked it to be strict about that.

sections.title: The Bandwidth Utilization Object
sections.content:
Link Bandwidth Utilization (LBU) is populated in the TED from the unidirectional utilized bandwidth sub-TLV. For a link or forwarding adjacency it is the actual utilization as measured in the router; for a bundled link it is the sum of the component links, including traffic from both RSVP-TE and non-RSVP-TE label switched paths. As a percentage it is the utilized bandwidth divided by the maximum bandwidth, times 100.

Link Reserved Bandwidth Utilization (LRBU) considers only the RSVP-TE traffic. The traffic from non-RSVP-TE paths is found by subtracting the available bandwidth from the residual bandwidth, and that value is deducted from the utilized bandwidth, so reserved bandwidth utilization equals utilized bandwidth minus (residual bandwidth minus available bandwidth). As a percentage it is that value divided by the maximum reservable bandwidth, times 100.

The BU object carries the upper limit of the acceptable link bandwidth utilization percentage. It has Object-Class 35 and Object-Type 1, and its body has a fixed length of 8 bytes: a 24-bit reserved field that must be set to zero and ignored on receipt, an 8-bit type field where 1 means LBU and 2 means LRBU, and a 32-bit bandwidth utilization value quantified as a percentage in IEEE floating point format.

A PCC that wants bandwidth utilization considered includes a BU object in its request, and a PCE that supports the object must ensure that no link on the computed path exceeds the given percentage. A message may carry several BU objects, as long as each is for a different utilization type; if it carries more than one of the same type, the first is processed and the rest are ignored. If the PCE does not support the object and the P bit is set, it must report an error and discard the request; if the P bit is cleared it may ignore the object. Use of the BU object for point-to-multipoint LSPs is outside the scope of the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The BU object sets a cap on how busy a link may be. It holds one byte for the type, one for the percentage and four reserved bytes, so it is 8 bytes long. The PCE must not return a path that uses a busier link than the cap. One cap can be set on the total traffic and another on the traffic that was reserved with RSVP-TE.

sections.title: Objective Functions
sections.content:
RFC 5541 defines the mechanism for specifying the objective function a PCE uses when it computes a path. The new path delay and path delay variation metrics can use the existing Minimum Cost Path objective function. For path loss the RFC defines a new one.

  • Objective Function Code 9, Minimum Packet Loss Path (MPLP): find a path P such that the percentage path loss PL(P) is minimized.
  • Objective Function Code 10, Maximum Under-Utilized Path (MUP): find a path P such that the smallest value of (M(Lpi) - u(Lpi)) / M(Lpi) over the links of the path is maximized, where u(L) is the bandwidth utilization of a link and M(L) its maximum bandwidth.
  • Objective Function Code 11, Maximum Reserved Under-Utilized Path (MRUP): find a path P such that the smallest value of (R(Lpi) - ru(Lpi)) / R(Lpi) over the links is maximized, where ru(L) is the reserved bandwidth utilization and R(L) the maximum reservable bandwidth.

If a PCE does not know the objective functions defined here, the procedure of Section 3.1.1 of RFC 5541 applies.
sections.plainLanguage: The objective function is the rule the PCE follows when several paths are possible. This RFC adds three: one that picks the path with the least packet loss, and two that pick the path whose busiest link has the most room left, counting either all traffic or only the reserved traffic.

sections.title: Reoptimizing Paths After a Degradation
sections.content:
RFC 6374 defines the measurement of loss, delay and related metrics over LSPs. When a PCC detects that network performance has degraded, either against the constraint it gave when the path was set up or against an implementation-specific threshold, it may ask the PCE to reoptimize the path by sending a request with the R bit set in the RP object.

A PCC can also notice the degradation without measuring anything, by watching the TED as populated by the IGP for changes in the performance parameters of the links that carry its LSPs. It can then ask for reoptimization of the affected LSPs. For example, if the bandwidth utilization of a link on the path drops below the value required when the path was set up, the PCC can send a reoptimization request to the PCE.

A stateful PCE can also decide which LSPs should be reoptimized, based on network events or on triggers from external monitoring systems. When a link deteriorates and its loss increases, that can lead the stateful PCE to work out which LSPs are affected and should be reoptimized.
sections.plainLanguage: A path that met its limits when it was set up can stop meeting them later. The client can notice that by measuring the path or by watching the link data in the database, and ask for a new path. A stateful path computation element can also notice the change and start the reoptimization itself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The new METRIC types, the BU object and the new objective function codes add no security concerns of their own beyond those discussed in RFC 5440 and RFC 5541.

Some deployments may find the service-aware information, such as delay and packet loss, to be extra sensitive, and it could be used to influence path computation and setup with adverse effect. Snooping PCEP messages that carry this data, or using PCEP messages for network reconnaissance, may give an attacker sensitive information about how the network operates. Such a deployment should use a suitable PCEP security mechanism, such as the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO) or PCEP security. The procedure based on Transport Layer Security in PCEP security is treated as a security enhancement and is much better suited to the sensitive service-aware information.
sections.plainLanguage: The new objects do not create new security problems, but the data they carry is worth protecting. Delay and loss figures can tell an attacker how the network is used, so the PCEP session itself should be secured, and the RFC prefers the method built on TLS.
